question: How does the SI define a metre? Give the speed-of-light value.

message.content:
The SI defines the metre as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of exactly 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition was adopted in 1983 and was refined in the 2019 revision of the SI system, which explicitly states that the metre is defined by fixing the numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum, *c*, to be exactly 299,792,458 when expressed in the SI unit m⋅s⁻¹ [4]. The second is defined based on the hyperfine transition frequency of the caesium-133 atom, Δ*ν*<sub>Cs</sub> [1][4].

The speed of light in vacuum, *c*, is defined as exactly 299,792,458 m/s within the SI system [1][2][3][4].

passages.heading: In unit systems
passages.text:
## In unit systems

The constant *c* is defined in the International System of Units (SI) as *exactly* 299792458 m/s. This fixed value is used to define the metre as exactly the distance that light travels in vacuum in 1⁄299792458 of a second. The second is, in turn, defined to be the length of time occupied by 9192631770 cycles of the radiation emitted by a caesium-133 atom in a transition between two specified energy states.<sup>[15]</sup> By using the fixed value of *c* and an accurate measurement of the second, the value for the standard metre is defined.<sup>[16]</sup>

passages.heading: Defined as an explicit constant
passages.text: As a result of this definition, the value of the speed of light in vacuum is exactly 299792458 m/s<sup>[172]</sup><sup>[173]</sup> and has become a defined constant in the SI system of units.<sup>[16]</sup> Improved experimental techniques that, prior to 1983, would have measured the speed of light no longer affect the known value of the speed of light in SI units, but instead allow a more precise realization of the metre by more accurately measuring the wavelength of krypton-86 and other light sources.<sup>[174]</sup><sup>[175]</sup>

passages.heading: Defined as an explicit constant
passages.text: In 2011, the CGPM stated its intention to redefine all seven SI base units using what it calls "the explicit-constant formulation", where each "unit is defined indirectly by specifying explicitly an exact value for a well-recognized fundamental constant", as was done for the speed of light. It proposed a new, but completely equivalent, wording of the metre's definition: "The metre, symbol m, is the unit of length; its magnitude is set by fixing the numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum to be equal to exactly 299792458 when it is expressed in the SI unit m s<sup>−1</sup>."<sup>[176]</sup> This was one of the changes that was incorporated in the 2019 revision of the SI, also termed the *New SI*.<sup>[177]</sup>

passages.heading: The Metre and the Speed of Light
passages.text:
## The Metre and the Speed of Light

A major change occurred in **1983**, when the metre was redefined in terms of the speed of light.

The modern definition states that:

**The metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299,792,458 of a second.**

This definition connects the metre with the speed of light in vacuum.

The speed of light in vacuum is assigned the exact value:

**c = 299,792,458 m/s**

The value is exact rather than an experimentally measured approximation within the SI system.

This means that if the speed of light and the duration of one second are known, the metre can be realized through the distance light travels during a precisely defined fraction of a second.

passages.heading: Why Is the Speed of Light Used?
passages.text:
## Why Is the Speed of Light Used?

The speed of light is an important constant in modern physics. According to Einstein’s theory of special relativity, light in vacuum travels at the same speed for all inertial observers, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.

Using this constant to define the metre provides several advantages.

First, the definition does not depend on a particular physical object. A laboratory does not need to possess an original metre bar to determine the unit.

Second, the definition can be reproduced using precise technologies such as lasers, optical frequency measurements, and advanced timing systems.

Third, the definition connects length measurement with time measurement. Since the speed of light has an exact value, extremely precise measurements of time can be used to establish extremely precise measurements of length.

passages.heading: FAQs
passages.text: The speed of light in vacuum is a fundamental constant of nature with an exact value in the SI system. Using it to define the metre provides a highly stable and reproducible standard. A physical object can potentially change because of damage, temperature, contamination, or other effects. The speed of light, however, provides a universal reference. By combining the exact speed of light with the precise definition of the second, scientists can establish the metre with extremely high accuracy. This approach is particularly valuable for advanced physics, engineering, manufacturing, astronomy, and precision measurement.

# Metre

| metre |  | 
|---|---|
| General information |  | 
| Unit system | SI | 
| Unit of | length | 
| Symbol | m <sup>[1]</sup> | 
| Conversions |  |

| Nautical units | ≈ 0.00053996 nmi | 

The **metre** (or **meter** in US spelling; symbol: **m**) is the base unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). Since 2019, the metre has been defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of 1/299792458 of a second, where the second is defined by a hyperfine transition frequency of caesium.<sup>[3]</sup>

The metre was originally defined in 1791 by the French National Assembly as one ten-millionth of the distance from the equator to the North Pole along a great circle through Paris, setting 10000 km as that quarter of the Earth's polar circumference.

passages.heading: Metre
passages.text: In 1799, the metre was redefined in terms of a prototype metre bar. The bar used was changed in 1889, and in 1960 the metre was redefined in terms of a certain number of wavelengths of a certain emission line of krypton-86. The current definition was adopted in 1983 and modified slightly in 2002 to clarify that the metre is a measure of proper length. From 1983 until 2019, the metre was formally defined as the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum in 1/299792458 of a second. After the 2019 revision of the SI, this definition was rephrased to include the definition of a second in terms of the caesium frequency Δ*ν*<sub>Cs</sub>.

passages.heading: History of definition
passages.text:
The metre, symbol m, is the SI unit of length. It is defined by taking the fixed numerical value of the speed of light in vacuum c to be 299792458 when expressed in the unit m⋅s<sup>−1</sup>, where the second is defined in terms of the caesium frequency Δ*ν*<sub>Cs</sub>.

Where older traditional length measures are still used, they are now defined in terms of the metre – for example the yard has since 1959 officially been defined as exactly 0.9144 metre.<sup>[20]</sup><sup>[21]</sup>

The intergovernmental organization, the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (*Bureau international des poids et mesures*, BIPM), was also established at that time. Located just outside of Paris in Sèvres, France, the BIPM serves as the focal point through which its member states act on matters of metrological significance. It is the ultimate arbiter of the International System of Units (SI, *Système Internationale d'Unités*) and the repository of the physical measurement standards. The kilogram was the last of the artifact-based measurement standards in the SI. (On May 20, 2019, it was officially replaced with a new definition based on constants of nature.)

So, in 1960, the 11th CGPM agreed to a new definition of the meter as the “length equal to 1,650,763.73 wavelengths in vacuum of the radiation corresponding to the transition between the levels 2p<sup>10</sup> and 5d<sup>5</sup> of the krypton-86 atom.” In other words, when electrons of a common form of krypton make a specific jump in energy, they release that energy in the form of reddish-orange light with a wavelength of 605.8 nanometers. Add up 1,650,753.73 of those wavelengths and you’ve got a meter.

But the krypton standard was not to endure for too long. (Sorry, Superman.) That’s because NIST scientists quickly developed another superhero-like power: the ability to reliably and precisely measure the fastest speed in the universe, namely, the speed of light in vacuum.

Building upon these and other advances, the meter was redefined by international agreement in 1983 as the length of the path traveled by light in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition also locked the speed of light at 299,792,458 meters per second in a vacuum. Length was now no longer an independent standard but rather was derived from the extremely accurate standard of time and a newly defined value for the speed of light made possible by the technology developed at NIST.

And thus, the meter has and likely will remain so elegantly defined in these terms for the foreseeable future.
